newsitem.title: UK: Australian PM plays down extreme right threat.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM plays down extreme right threat.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Friday that only a minority in his country held extreme right-wing views and he strongly denied that Australia was a racist state.

Interviewed on BBC radio during a visit to Britain, Howard also said the question of whether Australia should become a republic was not a front-line issue but there was still a "significant division of opinion" on it.
Howard was questioned about the views of Pauline Hanson whose One Nation party has attracted sizeable support by claiming Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.
"You have a certain amount of right-wingery in all western countries...and I think on a scale of 10 extreme views in Australia are lower than they are in many other countries," Howard said.

"There's nothing unusual in western society in people expressing extreme views from time to time. The views that she (Hanson) expresses are minority views, and any suggestion that Australia is a racist country is one that I repudiate completely."
Turning to the aboriginal problem, Howard said the policy of his government was to look forward and not back at the indignities heaped on Australia's indigenous population.

"It is not true of anyone to say that the Australian Aborigines are not disadvantaged as an identifiable group -- they are clearly a very disadvantaged people and the philosophy of my government rather than dwelling on the past is to focus on remedying current disadvantage as we go into the future," he said.

Howard is due to have lunch at Windsor Castle on Friday with Queen Elizabeth who is head of state of Australia. A convention on the question of whether Australia should become a republic is due to be held in December.
Howard declined to say whether he would discuss the subject with the queen but said the place of the monarchy in Australia was obviously very different from what it was 30 or 40 years ago.
"It's one of those issues that is bubbling along in the background. There's still a significant division of opinion but ultimately there will be a vote on it," he said.
"Whatever happens on that front, the bilateral relationship between Australia and Britain will remain very strong. It's not a front burner issue."
